en: New Commentary on the *Ullambana Sūtra* Spoken by the Buddha Compiled and Revised by the Bodhisattva Śrāmaṇera Zhixu of Gusu and the Bodhisattva Bhikṣu Daofang of Wenling.
This sutra is titled "The Dharma Offering. Its essence is the Three Jewels of intrinsic nature; its central principle is filial piety and compassion;

its function is to uproot suffering and bestow happiness; and its doctrinal character is that of the Mahāyāna. Originally, among the fields of merit in the human world, none is more esteemed than the Three Jewels;

among the dharmas of the supramundane path, none precedes filial piety and compassion. If one wishes to repay profound kindness, nothing is more essential than bestowing happiness and uprooting suffering.
In seeking to accomplish the salvation of beings, nothing is greater than the *Ullambana*. Therefore, when Maudgalyāyana’s Way was perfected, he first contemplated the kindness of his nursing mother;
the Great Sage, bestowing compassion, extensively revealed the ritual for the Dharma-offering. The time must be chosen during the *Pravāraṇā*, and the merit relies upon the assembly of monks.
Where the Jewel of the Sangha resides, there the Wheel of Dharma abides; wherever the Wheel of Dharma turns, the Buddha is ever present.

Manifest before us, the one raised up is the three; most supreme and peerless. With a single utterance of his perfect voice, the Compassionate Father was already liberated from the wheel of suffering.
His grace extended to all by way of analogy, and his fragrant path was perpetually bequeathed to both the ordained and the laity. Who does not have parents? How could one fail to reflect upon this?

All the more so, since he has left behind such earnest instructions, commanding that we constantly remember them in every thought-moment. Unless one observes the mind and gives rise to [realization]...
Practice! How could it be that both principle and phenomena are not simultaneously revealed? This single-character Dharma-gate is beyond the capacity of oceans of ink to exhaustively record;
it is the bridge for the fourfold assembly to cross together—how could it be a mere shallow or mundane path? I shall briefly outline five stages to explore its profound essence.
Within these five stages, each further clarifies the meaning in two ways: first, in terms of phenomena (*dharma*), and second, through the contemplation of the mind (*citta*).
First, regarding the explanation of the name based on its function: this refers to the *Ullambana*, which is the name for the Dharma-offering (*dharma-pūjā*). *Ullambana* is a Sanskrit term;
in its original form it is *ullambana*. This translates as "rescuing those who hang head-downward," referring to the intense sufferings of the three miserable realms (*tridurgati*).
It is beyond description; I borrow the metaphor of being "suspended upside down. Once this Dharma is established, those who are suspended upside down shall be released, and this is termed "rescue.
The character *pen* (盆) is a Chinese term for a clean vessel used to store food; all bowls and basins are collectively called *pen*.
Later generations, failing to understand this, fashioned a single large platter upon which all the food was placed together for universal offering.

This would be a great violation of the monastic regulations, and the Sangha would not partake [of such offerings]. Although ordinary beings and sages differ, both alike must not touch the vessels used for the Sangha’s food.
What is now called the *Ullambana* (Almsgiving Bowl) refers to using various clean bowls and basins to store various clean, delicious foods and offering them to the Sangha of the ten directions;
thus one can rescue one's compassionate parents, who are like those hanging upside down.
Suffering is that which is to be rescued; the *pén* (vessel) is that which can rescue. When the "capable" and the "object" are combined, it is called the *Ullambana-pén*.

Furthermore, based on its function of rescuing from the state of being "upside-down suspended," this vessel is also named the "Vessel for Rescuing the Upside-Down Suspended. Now, regarding both the *pariccheda-vipariṇāma* (segmented transformation) and the *pariṇāmi-vipariṇāma* (transformative transformation)...

All are termed retributions of suffering. Why should it be only the hungry ghosts who are called "hanging upside down"? The four inversions of ordinary beings and the four inversions of the two vehicles are all causes of inversion.
In the desire realm, there is no food of meditative concentration; throughout the three realms of existence, one lacks the nectar of outflow-free wisdom.
To be biased toward the ultimate truth while lacking the conventional truth; to lose the Middle Way’s true flavor regarding the Dharma, wealth, and provisional status—all these are inverted fruits.
To take a bowl and almsbowl as a basin, and the hundred flavors and five fruits as food, is to resolve the inverted suspension of the hungry ghosts.

To take the collected mind as a basin and the ten branches [of the precepts] as food, is to resolve the inverted suspension of the desire realm. To take the foundations of mindfulness as a basin and the practice of contemplation on the Four Truths as food, is to resolve...

The three realms are inverted and suspended upside down. The great vow serves as the basin; the six perfections and myriad practices serve as the food. This resolves the inverted suspension of the four types of "withered" views.

A single mind serves as the basin; inconceivable contemplation serves as the food. This resolves the inverted suspension of the two extremes. By extending this principle, one may apply it to all similar categories.

In general, the hundred flavors served in bowls and alms-bowls constitute the objective conditions for the primary cause. If there were no objective realm of phenomena, the contemplation of principle would have nothing upon which to rely;
if there were no contemplation of principle, the efficacy of phenomena would not be profound.

If, upon hearing this teaching, one wishes to abolish the practice of phenomena, then why was it that even after Maudgalyāyana had first attained the six supernormal powers and had already perfected the vessel of the foundations of mindfulness and the food of the Four Noble Truths, his mother still did not [attain liberation]?

"Is one liberated from the realm of ghosts? The Buddha’s explanation of these two characters is as in the standard interpretation. That "sūtra" is a general name is also as explained in the standard commentaries; it shall not be described here at length.
Next, regarding the explanation of the name through the contemplation of the mind: with pure precepts as the vessel, there are the four truths of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*).

Inconceivable contemplative wisdom serves as its sustenance. By making offerings to the Three Jewels of the single essence of self-nature, one completely resolves the pendent errors of the eight inversions and suddenly treads upon the ground of the single reality.
The father of ignorance and the mother of craving are, in that very moment, transformed into clarity and liberation;
the mother of wisdom-perfection and the father of skillful means spontaneously enter the state of effortless non-action. Therefore, it is called the *Ullambana*.
Second, regarding the determination of the essence (*tattva*) based on the phenomena: all sūtras must necessarily possess a correct essence.

If they lacked a correct essence, they would be erroneous and inverted, lacking the seal (*mudrā*), and would thus become the teachings of Māra. Generally speaking, all Mahāyāna sūtras take the true reality (*bhūtata-lakṣaṇa*) as their seal and as the correct essence of the sūtra.
Although this true reality is one, it possesses various names, such as Śakra Devendra. One...
A single person may have many names, yet universally responds to all [who call]. The true mark (*dharmatā*) is likewise so: a single dharma has many names and universally responds to all sūtras.
Since the sūtras have distinct titles, it is logically no fault to invoke the universal essence by means of these specific names. Now, within this sūtra it says:
"One must rely upon the majestic spiritual power of the Saṃgha of the ten directions. It further says: "When first receiving food, one should first establish..."
Before the Buddha, after the monks had finished their ritual invocation for blessings, he then personally received the food. This invocation is itself the Dharma;
it is the complete fulfillment of the Triple Gem. Maudgalyāyana also said: "One receives the power of the merit of the Triple Gem.

Furthermore, this Triple Gem is the very self-nature of all sentient beings. If the self-nature of sentient beings did not inherently possess the merit of the Triple Gem, [then this would not be possible].

Thus, the ordinary and the sagely would be separated by distinct barriers, and light and darkness would diverge forever. The ordinary would be unable to evoke a response, and the sagely could not provide a response.
This is because the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are non-different in their threefold nature; although delusion and enlightenment differ, their essential substance is eternally one.

Therefore, when sentient beings within the minds of all Buddhas rely on phenomena to entrust themselves to principle and evoke the Buddhas within the minds of sentient beings, then [the sentient beings...]
The Buddhas within the mind are without conditions or conceptual thought; they respond spontaneously to sentient beings within the minds of all Buddhas.
Therefore, the self-nature Three Jewels constitute the essence of this sutra. To explain these self-nature Three Jewels, there are four further meanings.

First, the Three Jewels of Sustenance; second, the Three Jewels of Ultimate Meaning; third, the Three Jewels of Distinct Characteristics of the Mahāyāna; and fourth, the Three Jewels of the Single Essence.
Regarding the Three Jewels of Sustenance: when the Buddha was in the world, his attainment of the Way beneath the King of Trees constituted the Jewel of the Buddha.
The teaching of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths is the Jewel of the Dharma. The ordination of the five bhikṣus is the Jewel of the Saṃgha.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, images fashioned from cast metal or molded clay, and those depicted on paper and silk with ink and colors, constitute the Jewel of the Buddha. The yellow scrolls and red tablets containing the holy teachings of the Tripiṭaka constitute the Jewel of the Dharma.
Those who shave their hair, don dyed robes, and continue to propagate the Buddha’s transformation constitute the Jewel of the Saṃgha. These three shall remain in the world without interruption.
Therefore, they are called the "Abiding Three Jewels. One should know that all images are the True Body (dharmakāya);
wherever the scriptures are located, that is the relic of the Dharma-body;

and even ordinary bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs are able to uphold the True Dharma and serve as fields of merit for the world—worthy of honor and esteem—they are all termed "Jewels," which cannot be adequately illustrated by worldly treasures.
Regarding the Three Jewels of the Ultimate Truth: the qualities of the All-Knowing One beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), consisting of the five aggregates, are called the Jewel of the Buddha.
The sixteen-foot golden body is merely a vessel that carries these teachings and the Dharma; the images of the present day are likewise symbols of this vessel that carries the Way.
The cessation of desire and the state of desirelessness—the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) and Nirvāṇa—are not [confined to] the three periods of time.
That which is subsumed therein, whose nature is eternally abiding, is called the Dharma Jewel. The sound of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths merely serves to explain this ultimate truth;

likewise, the yellow scrolls and red tablets serve as the means to transmit this sound of the Dharma and also explain this ultimate truth, enabling people to perceive the Path through words—just as fish and hares rely on the trap and snare, or as one relies on a pointing finger to see the bright moon.
The virtues of the Śrāvakas, both those in training and those beyond training, are called the Saṃgha Jewel. The six rules for communal harmony merely refer to those who are treading toward this path.
As for the distinct characteristics of the Three Jewels in the Mahāyāna, they sit upon lotus pedestals, having perfected the path of initial awakening (ādikṣānti).

The true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is equal [to all], eternally abiding and never ceasing. Adorned with the marks and signs as numerous as the atoms of a buddha-field, it manifests countless transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) to universally deliver all sentient beings;
this is the Jewel of the Buddha. The twelve divisions of the sūtras constitute the truly pure treasury of Dharma.
Each individual sūtra has for its retinue unspeakably unspeakable numbers of sūtras, and each single syllable of the Dharma...
The gates [of the Dharma] could not be fully recorded even if one were to write with ink as vast as the ocean; this is the Jewel of the Dharma (*dharmaratna*).

The Three Sages and Ten Saints possess sovereign supernatural powers that pervade the ten directions; they seek enlightenment above and transform beings below through the two kinds of adornment—merit and wisdom.

All who behold their forms or hear their names obtain supreme benefit; this is the Jewel of the Sangha (*saṃgharatna*). As for the "Three Jewels in One Essence," through the wisdom of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇaprajñā*), one awakens.

To fully comprehend all phenomena as being neither empty nor existent, yet both empty and existent—wherein both negation and affirmation are simultaneously forgotten and simultaneously illumined—is the perfect awakening of the three wisdoms, which is called the Buddha Jewel.
The principle of the dharma-nature that is thus awakened, wherein the three truths are fully present, is called the Dharma Jewel.
This very awakening-wisdom, when in harmony with both principle and phenomena, is called the Sangha Jewel. These three are not separate entities; one should know this as well.

This refers to the three paths, the three consciousnesses, the three causes, the three knowledges, the three enlightenments, the three Great Vehicles, the three bodies, the three nirvāṇas, the three virtues, and so forth.
They are neither one nor three; yet they are three and they are one. They do not diminish in ordinary beings, nor do they increase in sages.
They have existed inherently from the beginning and are not merely something acquired now. Although they are fundamentally complete, those in delusion do not realize it; however—
There is a principle here; this is the Buddha as Principle (*li-jì*). It is also called the Dharma as Principle, and also called the Sangha as Principle.

Whether one hears this from a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) or hears it from the sūtras, once heard, one attains understanding and realization, as if awakening from a dream, with no further doubt or confusion.
This is the Three Jewels as Name (*míng-zì*). Contemplating the mind according to this principle and perfectly subduing the five stages of dwelling (*wǔ zhù*) is called "Contemplation" (*guān*).

The practice of the Three Jewels: when a semblance understanding arises, the six sense organs become purified, the afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) fall away first, and the delusions as numerous as motes of dust are also exhausted;
this is called the Semblance Three Jewels. When the divisions of ignorance are shattered and one accords with the true and eternal, it is called the Partially True Three Jewels.
When Bodhi is perfected and the self-nature of all phenomena is realized, such that body and land are of one essence and principle and phenomena are equal, it is called the Ultimate Three Jewels.
These four meanings, though differing in depth, trace their origin and culminate in the self-nature (*svabhāva*).

Although the last [meaning] realizes the self-nature, it never abandons the first three; and although the first three have not yet reached the self-nature, they never exist apart from that nature as separate establishments.
Therefore, they are collectively termed the "Self-Nature Triple Gem" (*svabhāva-triratna*). This self-nature...
The Jewel. It is the true essence of a single sutra, the great confluence of all dharmas. All manner of myriad practices converge toward it;
immeasurable merits collectively adorn it; and through speech and debate, it is elucidated and revealed.
Like a father, like a sovereign, like the moon, like the ocean, and like Śakra, Lord of Devas—it is most honored and most noble; therefore, it is called the "essence" (*tattva*). Furthermore, this...
The Three Jewels are the very source and foundation of all phenomena (*dharmas*).

If one can deeply understand the meaning of these Three Jewels, one will have exhausted the source and foundation of all phenomena, with no further remainder; therefore, they are called the "essence" (*tattva*).
Furthermore, by realizing these Three Jewels, one is able to universally penetrate all dharma-gates, for there is not even the slightest phenomenon that exists outside of the Three Jewels.

Because there is not even the slightest phenomenon that does not fully possess the essential nature of the Three Jewels, they are called the "Essence. Sentient beings are deluded regarding this essence of the Three Jewels;
thus, though not actually turning their backs on it, they turn their backs upon it, giving rise to afflictions and creating karma.

Consequently, they give birth to the suffering and origin of the ten realms, as well as to perversions—whether clinging to the outflows (*sāsrava*), clinging to the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), clinging to the two extremes, or clinging to...
The Middle Way is collectively termed stinginess and greed, like those hungry ghosts. The Sage awakens to the essential nature of these Three Jewels;

therefore, he accords with them while not being bound by them. By cultivating causes, he realizes the fruit, giving rise to all paths—whether partial or complete, sudden or gradual—and their respective cessations.

He destroys the obstacles of evil karma, the obstacles of views and afflictions, the obstacles of the sands of *saṃsāra*, and the obstacle of ignorance. This is collectively termed the "Dharma-offering."

Just as with Maudgalyāyana, the essence of the sūtra is therefore taken to be the Three Jewels of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Next, regarding the discernment of the essence through the contemplation of the mind:
it is precisely this sentient being’s present single thought-moment of the nature of cognitive awareness. It is neither internal nor external; it does not abide in between.
It is neither past nor present, nor is it future. It is not blue, yellow, red, or white; it is not long, short, square, or [round].
Perfectly round, it is without beginning or end vertically and transcends all boundaries horizontally. If one wishes to say it exists, there is not even a trace of it;

if one wishes to say it does not exist, it cannot be annihilated. It is fundamentally free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), yet due to failing to perceive its own essence, one becomes deluded.
Although one has long accumulated this immersion in confusion, it never undergoes any diminution or deficiency. This is called the Buddha Jewel, manifesting before all.
The ten realms, including both the environment and its inhabitants, are all manifestations within this momentary mind.
Just as the various phenomena perceived in a dream do not ultimately depart from the dreaming mind, so too it is with all phenomena appearing before us now.
Although it is falsely claimed that these exist as distinct realities external to one's own mind, they do not actually exist at all.
They are just like when one has not yet awakened from a dream and clings to the dream as real; once awake, however, one searches for them and finds they cannot be obtained.
In this same way, the ten realms manifested within the mind do not depart from one's own mind; this is called the Dharma Jewel. There is no dharma outside the mind, and no mind outside the dharmas.

Leave it to the confusion and delusion of inversion; one may distinguish between subject and object, yet ultimately, when seeking dharmas apart from the mind, not even a hair’s breadth of a dharma-characteristic can be found.
When seeking the mind apart from dharmas, likewise not even the slightest characteristic of mind can be found.

Thus, the mind is itself the dharma, and the dharma is itself the mind. They have been in harmony from the beginning and cannot be separated; this is called the Sangha Jewel. This is the essential point.
Within a single thought-moment, the essential nature of these Three Jewels is perfectly complete, lacking nothing and exceeding nothing;
it is like a vajra, indestructible and imperishable. As it is with one thought-moment, so it is with all thought-moments.
All Buddhas rely upon this to attain the Way, turn the Great Wheel of Dharma, and enter Great Nirvana; it is that which sustains all things.
The Three Jewels: the ultimate Three Jewels, the Three Jewels of distinct characteristics, and the Three Jewels of the single essence. Because they are established by means of these, it is said:
"All sentient beings possess the characteristic of nirvāṇa; they do not undergo further extinction. It is also said: "The liberation of all Buddhas..."
One should seek it within the mental activities of sentient beings. If one can contemplate this infinitesimal moment of mind (*citta*), then one will be able to fulfill all Buddha-dharmas.
Therefore it is said: "The ocean of the Tathāgatas' right and universal knowledge arises from the mind and its thoughts.
If one does not perform this contemplation of the mind to discern its essence, how could one be said to constantly remember one's parents in every thought-moment?
And how does one cultivate filial piety and compassion?

Third, clarifying the essence through its manifestations: although precepts are immeasurable, they take filial piety as their essence; although myriad practices are numerous, they take filial piety as their foremost priority.
This is why Śākyamuni, throughout kalpas of vast duration, constantly cultivated the practice of repaying kindness, and why Maudgalyāyana attained the Way.
One should immediately reflect upon the kindness of nursing and suckling. It should be understood that it is not only after attaining the Way that one remembers one's parents;
rather, it is precisely because of the causal conditions for repaying parental kindness that one cultivates the Noble Path.

For example, when the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha was formerly a Brahmin girl, she gave rise to the mind of great compassion in order to deliver her mother, vowing that as long as the realms of sentient beings were not empty, she would not first attain Buddhahood herself.
The causes and conditions for the initial resolve of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are generally like this. In expounding upon this filial piety and righteousness, there are two types:
first, worldly filial piety; second, world-transcending filial piety. Worldly filial piety has three aspects: first, being able to honor one's parents.
This means: first, to personally become a sage or worthy and thereby be able to serve as an exemplar for one's parents on the Path, such as the Great Shun;

second, to carry on their will and continue their undertakings, such as King Wu and the Duke of Zhou; third, not to bring disgrace upon one's parents, such as Zengzi’s laying out his hands and feet [in death];
and fourth, to be able to nourish one's parents, such as the requirement of having wine and meat. One who can thus honor their parents is called "greatly filial. Furthermore—
This is called "attaining filial piety" and is also called "ultimate filial piety"; it is the pinnacle of worldly filial piety.

Yet, although the ancestral temple may offer sacrifices for it and descendants may preserve its legacy, it cannot cause one's parents to escape the suffering of saṃsāra and realize the bliss of the eternal abiding.

The Sages established their teachings by following the dispositions of sentient beings with flexibility. The "willow leaves" that stop a child’s crying serve as a prologue for the filial piety that transcends the world.
This transcendental filial piety, moreover, has two meanings: first, directly clarifying the way of filial piety; second, accomplishing filial piety through compassion.
Regarding the direct clarification of the way of filial piety, there are four types: first, providing offerings with one's whole heart; second, guiding others to cultivate goodness; third...
Exhorting them to abandon evil; fourth, causing them to realize the fruits of the Path. Regarding "serving with all one's heart," as the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:

"If a person were to carry their father on the right shoulder and their mother on the left shoulder for a hundred years, providing them with the finest worldly delicacies, clothing, and food, they still could not repay even a moment’s worth of their kindness.
From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to serve [their parents] with all their hearts."
One should serve one’s parents for as long as life lasts; if one fails to do so, one incurs a grave offense.

Regarding the inducement to practice virtue, as stated in the *Xiaozijing* (Sutra on Filial Sons) spoken by the Buddha: "If one cannot transform one's parents through the ultimate [teachings] of the Three Honored Ones..."

Even if one exhausts oneself in filial support, it is still considered unfilial if one cannot cause one’s parents to abandon evil and practice goodness, to uphold the five precepts and maintain the three refuges, and to live in devotion until their final moments. The *Vinayamātṛkā-sūtra* states:
"If one's parents are poor, first grant them the refuges and the precepts, and only thereafter provide material gifts; furthermore, one should personally cultivate wholesome deeds."

Practicing [these precepts] is also called filial piety. As the *Maimayi jing* (Sūtra on the Intention of Insult) says: "When a person upholds the precepts, they are thereby filially obedient and repaying the kindness of their parents.
Why is this? By not killing living beings, one attains longevity; by not stealing, one is wealthy; by being free from lust and disorder, one is not confused;
by not deceiving, one is trusted; and by not drinking alcohol, one is pure. There are times when one's parents fall into these states, and [the child can rescue them]."
This means peace and security. Regarding the exhortation to abandon evil, the *Xiaozijing* (Classic of Filial Piety) states:

"If one's parents are obstinate and ignorant, failing to revere the Triple Gem, or are cruel, tyrannical, and violent, the child should offer earnest admonitions to enlighten them. If they still do not awaken,"
He immediately sought to transform them. Taking their arms and leading his kin, he showed them the prison of the sovereign and the punishments and executions of the various prisoners.
If they still did not change, he wept and wailed with grief, refusing all food and drink. Though his parents were ignorant, they must surely have feared for their son’s death;

thus, they should have forced themselves to endure and submit, cherishing the Right Way in their hearts. The rites of Confucianism also state: "If one's parents have faults, one should remonstrate with them three times."
If they do not grant permission, one should follow them while wailing and weeping.
Those who have realized the fruit of the Way are like Jingzang and Jingyan toward King Miaozhuangyan, or Śākyamuni Buddha toward his father, King Śuddhodana, and likewise Queen Māyā and others.
These four types of filial piety accord with the intent of the four *siddhāntas*. The first type is identical [to the first *siddhānta*].
In the world, the third type of filial care is that which brings joy and benefit to one's parents;

however, such worldly filial piety often involves killing living beings, thereby creating heavy karmic bonds of enmity. Transcendental filial care is pure and faultless; this is the distinction between them.
Cultivating good and abandoning evil is equivalent to the greatest filial piety in the world, enabling one’s parents to give rise to wholesome states.

The eradication of evil brings two benefits. If one personally cultivates virtuous conduct, this is also called filial piety; it is equivalent to the second worldly way of not bringing disgrace upon one's parents.
However, while Confucianism clarifies "not bringing disgrace" only with respect to the present life, the power of the Buddha’s precepts delivers beings through many kalpas.
This is the distinction. It enables the realization of the fruits of the Path, which is something the world lacks, and can cause one's parents to attain [liberation].
Regarding the benefit of entering into principle: the first three [periods] constitute the provisional, while this one constitutes the real.

Within the entry into principle, there are further distinctions of the provisional and the real based on birth-and-death, non-arising, the immeasurable, and the unconditioned; these meanings are inexhaustible. In the present sutra, from the perspective of the traces (*traces*), it generally belongs to the provisional;
yet from the perspective of the teaching and the principle, it must certainly be returned to the real. Never before has there been such a compassionate plea to bring about deliverance.

Although they turn the wheel of suffering, they nonetheless remain ultimately stalled at the false fruits of the human and celestial realms. Next, the explanation of accomplishing filial piety through compassion is further divided into three parts:
first, compassion based on sentient beings; second, compassion based on dharmas; and third, unconditioned compassion. Regarding compassion based on sentient beings:
Contemplate all sentient beings as one would think of one's own parents. Thus, the Brahmajāla Sūtra states:
"All men are my fathers; all women are my mothers. In every successive birth, there is none from whom I have not received life.
When one contemplates in this way, enemies and kin are regarded with equality, and one bestows the three grades of happiness upon the seven types of objects in succession. By means of this—
Subduing anger, affliction, stinginess, and envy, one even attains the *maitrī-citta-samādhi*.

For all those with whom I share a karmic connection, I am able to extract their suffering and bestow happiness upon them. Because the debt of parental kindness is the most profound, they are the first to be granted this extraction of suffering.
Regarding "compassion for phenomena" (*dharma-maitrī*), one contemplates that all phenomena arise from conditions; thus, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* says: "One..."
All earth and water are my former bodies; all fire and wind are my fundamental substance. Sentient beings are composed solely of these four great elements (*mahābhūta*);
there is no self and no person, no life-span and no soul. Since the four great elements are non-dual, the objects of one's compassionate mind are likewise non-dual.
When practicing this contemplation, enemies and kin appear as a single aspect, until one attains realization.
The power of the samādhi of loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta*) that uproots [afflictions] is even more superior than the former. Regarding "unconditioned loving-kindness" (*apratihata-maitrī*):

one realizes that the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are non-differentiated; that the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is of a single characteristic (*eka-lakṣaṇa*), truly equal, and abides neither in the marks of phenomena (*dharma-nimitta*) nor in the marks of sentient beings (*sattva-nimitta*).
One contemplates that awakening (*bodhi*) is itself affliction (*kleśa*), and nirvāṇa is itself birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), thereby giving rise to the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
The vow: wishing to uproot the suffering of inherent nature, one contemplates that afflictions are themselves bodhi and birth-and-death are themselves nirvana;
thus one gives rise to the vow of non-action. Wishing to bestow the bliss of inherent nature, this compassion is itself pity and this pity is itself compassion.

This is the perfect cultivation in accordance with the nature, which perfumes and brings forth samādhi. Following the capacities and conditions of sentient beings throughout the dharma-realm, it accords with those who may be transformed.
One who realizes the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) acts spontaneously and responds without deliberation or calculation. Such great compassion is inconceivable;

it manifests through the universal gate (samantamukha), its spiritual power being boundless. There is not a single sentient being among those contained within the dust-motes of all lands who is not universally delivered.

Since it gives birth to such profound virtue, how could one not attain transcendence? These three types of compassion—beginning with that based on conditions (ālambana)—are shared by the practitioners of the Three Vehicles.
As for cultivation: because the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) originally lack the great vow to benefit others, their power is slight;

when Bodhisattvas cultivate it, its efficacy is vast and great. Next is the compassion based on dharmas (dharmālambana-maitrī); this can also be practiced to a small degree by the two vehicles, yet it is precisely what Bodhisattvas cultivate.
Third is the compassion without an object (anālambana-maitrī), which belongs to the Middle Way of the Buddha-dharma and is not shared with the two vehicles. Now, regarding Maudgalyāyana...

The commentator must explain this in terms of the fundamental (hon) and the provisional (jaku). Fundamentally, all the great śrāvakas are manifestations of the Dharma-body who have long practiced and long realized unconditioned great compassion (*nirālamba-mahāmaitrī*).
Provisionally, they manifest as having attained only the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle, possessing merely the power of compassion for sentient beings (*sattvālambana-maitrī*).

Therefore, the Buddha distinguished them, saying: "This is not something that can be accomplished by the power of you alone. The Way of the various sages is fully endowed with these three kinds of compassion.
Therefore it is said: "One must rely on the power of the Sangha of the ten directions. Why is filial piety established by means of the three types of compassion? As the sutra states:

"Always with filial compassion, one should remember one's parents who gave birth to one. One should know that if the power of compassion is not cultivated, the way of filial piety will not be perfected.
Confucianists also say: "To harm even a single insect without cause is not filial; to [harm] without cause..."

To damage even a single blade of grass or tree is not filial piety; how much more so is this the case regarding the Buddha-dharma? Furthermore, compassion is itself compliance, for it accords with the *dharmatā*.
Compliance is filial piety, and filial piety is the essential core of all Buddha-dharma. Those who wish to be filial to their parents [must practice compassion].
One must accord with the Three Jewels. Desiring to be filial toward the Three Jewels, one must cultivate filial piety and compassion to repay the kindness of one's parents.
Furthermore, the Three Jewels are themselves one's parents. As the *Mawei yi jing* (Sūtra on the Meaning of Insult) states: "The Buddha is the father; the Dharma is the mother," and so forth.
Moreover, one's parents are also the Three Jewels. As it is said: "There are two living Buddhas within your home," referring to the father and [the mother].

Mother. Thus, the Brahmajāla Sūtra says: "Be filial toward one's parents, teachers, monks, and the Triple Gem; be filial toward the Dharma of the Ultimate Way. The present sutra takes filial piety and compassion as its central theme.
Next, regarding the clarification of the central theme through the contemplation of the mind: within the single thought-moment of the present, the Triple Gem is fully present.
To observe this in accordance with reality is called "filial piety"; it is also termed the "Dharma-offering. As for wandering in delusion:
This is called "rebellion" and is also termed the "root of sin. If for a single thought-moment one accords with contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā*), then all ten realms are simultaneously awakened;
how much more so one's parents? If for a single thought-moment one turns one's back on the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), then all ten realms are simultaneously deluded;

how could it stop at one's parents alone? Furthermore, awakening means that Prajñāpāramitā is the mother and Upāya is the father, both attaining liberation. Delusion, however, leaves one without [these].

The father represents craving; the mother represents attachment. Together they return to the wheel of suffering. To contemplate the mind in this way is to constantly cultivate filial piety and compassion within every thought-moment.

Fourth, regarding the application of function through phenomena: to extract suffering and bestow happiness constitutes its power and function. [It] extracts the suffering of hungry ghosts and bestows...
The bliss of rebirth in the heavens is merely a brief explanation based on what is proximate. In reality, it involves uprooting the suffering of birth and death and bestowing the bliss of nirvana;

uprooting the suffering of stagnation in quiescence and bestowing the bliss of sporting with supernatural powers; and uprooting the suffering of the two extremes and bestowing the bliss of the Middle Way.
Birth in the Land of Expedient Means is called the Heaven of Purity; birth in the Land of Retribution is called the Heaven of Meaning;
birth in the Land of Tranquil Light is called the God among Gods, the Heaven of Great Nirvana. To bestow [the benefit] in this manner is precisely the great power and function of the present sutra.
Next, regarding the application of the clarity of contemplating the mind: simply contemplate that the single thought-moment of the present is fully endowed with the Triple Gem.

As for its essential nature, it is able to perfectly uproot the suffering and its accumulation within the ten realms of one's own nature, and it perfectly bestows the path and cessation within the ten realms of one's own nature.

Fifth, regarding the classification of the teaching according to its phenomenal content: this is subsumed under the Mahāyāna Vaipulya (Extensive) teaching. As for the names and meanings of the two collections (piṭakas):
It is included within the Bodhisattva-piṭaka. The old [tradition] states that it belongs to the vehicle of humans and devas and is contained within the Hīnayāna-piṭaka;

however, this merely refers to the passage concerning attaining liberation from the realm of hungry ghosts and entering the Flower-Radiance Heaven. How could the Hīnayāna-piṭaka possibly clarify the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) of great beings?

Is it not a matter of the provisional manifestation as a bhikṣu and so forth? Someone asked: "When Maudgalyāyana first attained the six supernormal powers, it was precisely within the twelve years [of the Buddha's teaching].
How can the *Āgama* teachings be considered Vaipulya? He replied: "You only know of the five periods as distinct;

you do not know that there is a commonality among the five periods. One must rely on the underlying principles to determine the character of each division; only then will one be free from error. Next...

Regarding the characteristics of the teaching of contemplating the mind: the mind possesses all vehicles; the mind itself is the teaching; the mind is called the Mahāyāna because there is nothing it does not transport.

When the contemplation is perfected in a single thought-moment, it transforms the teaching for the subsequent thoughts and all mental factors and mental concomitants. This is what is meant by the characteristics of the teaching of contemplating the mind.
If one does not explain this in relation to concrete phenomena, one will not understand the significance of the Tathāgata’s path of teaching. If one does not contemplate...
Explanation of the Mind: One cannot always practice the Dharma-offering at all times. As the Sūtra says: "In every thought-moment, one should constantly keep one's parents and others in mind.
This is an instruction to contemplate the mind. Furthermore, it says: "On the fifteenth day of the seventh month of every year..."

"To prepare the *urubhanda* (alms-bowl) vessel" teaches the practice of making offerings. Furthermore, it says, "All disciples of the Buddha should uphold this Dharma," which is a dual exhortation to receive and maintain [the teaching].

This is truly because sentient beings, from beginningless time until now, have each possessed two kinds of ignorance—delusion regarding phenomena and delusion regarding principle—and each possesses two kinds of heavy obstructions—evil karma and afflictions. Therefore...

One must cultivate both principle and practice together; only then can one ultimately uproot suffering and bestow happiness. May the disciples of the Buddha reflect upon this and cultivate it accordingly.

The entry into the text is divided into three parts: first, the introductory section (*nidāna*); second, the main body of the teaching (*śarīra*); and third, the section on propagation (*pariṇāmana*). First, the introductory section.
II. First, the general introduction; second, the specific introduction.
Now, the first: Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The General Preface is also called the Preface of Certification and Faith. Because these words are uniformly placed at the beginning of all sūtras, it is named the "General Preface.
Because these six kinds of accomplishment certify that this is the Buddha’s teaching and cause sentient beings to give rise to faith, it is named the "Preface of Certification and Faith."
Thus have I heard. Or it is said: "Thus have I heard. In the Western Regions (India), inverted word order is frequently used;

translators each followed their own convenience, yet there is truly no difference in meaning. "Heard" means that Ānanda personally heard it from the Buddha and subsequently propagated it in accordance with worldly custom.
To designate a "self" by conventional name while conforming to the dharma of non-self is merely a matter of terminology; in its true meaning, there is no fixed location.

It is not different from the Name-as-Such (nāma-tathatā); there is nothing that is not called "this. When the capacity of the seeker and the response of the teacher strike one another, and the assembly for the Dharma is complete, it is called "one time" (ekasamaya).

One whose omniscience is perfected and whose awakening and practice are fulfilled is called a Buddha. By means of the four modes of dwelling, he manifests his traces among humans, demonstrating the same arising [as ordinary beings].

Regarding "abiding," it is said: "It exists. The four types of abidings are: the celestial abiding (*devasthāna*), the Brahma abiding (*brahmasthāna*), the noble abiding (*āryasthāna*), and the Buddha abiding (*buddhasthāna*).

The celestial abiding consists of generosity, ethical discipline, and a virtuous mind; these are the causes for the six heavens. The Brahma abiding consists of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity;

these are the causes for the realms of form and formlessness. The noble abiding consists of the three gates of liberation; these are the causes for the noble fruits of the three vehicles. The Buddha abiding is *Śūraṅgama*...
The [four] concentrations (*samādhi*), the powers (*bala*), the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), and so forth, are the dharmas for the Buddha’s own enjoyment.

The celestial abodes (*devasthāna*) and the Brahma abodes (*brahmasthāna*) correspond to ordinary beings; the noble abodes (*āryasthāna*) correspond to those of gradual capacity; and the Buddha-abode (*buddhasthāna*) corresponds to those of sudden capacity.

The Buddha is the person who dwells, while the four [abodes] are the dharmas in which he dwells. Furthermore, the four are the dharmas by which he dwells, while the lands, cities, gardens, and groves are the physical locations where he dwells.
Śrāvastī is the name of a great kingdom in the Western Regions; it is translated here as "Hearing Things" (聞物) and also as "Abundant Virtue" (豐德).
Jetavana Anāthapiṇḍada-ārāma was originally the garden of Prince Jeta. The elder Sudatta purchased it by scattering gold coins over the ground;
when there was a small portion of land remaining where he had not yet scattered them, the Prince immediately gave rise to a resolute mind and offered it [to the Sangha].
Because he practiced giving, the names of both individuals are mentioned together. Sudatta was fond of practicing charity and rescuing the orphaned and the solitary;

thus, people of the time called him Anāthapiṇḍada (Giver of Alms to the Destitute). On a matter of business, he traveled to Rājagṛha. Upon first hearing the name of the Buddha, the hairs on his body stood on end.
He contemplated this without sleeping, until the dark night became brightly illuminated. He resolved to go and see [the Buddha]; the massive gates opened of their own accord.

Having heard the Dharma and realized the fruit [of enlightenment], he invited the Buddha to transform and deliver the people of Śrāvastī; therefore, he spread gold to purchase a grove and constructed a saṃghārāma.
Within this, the word "hearing" (śruta) refers to the accomplishment of hearing; likewise, it refers to the accomplishment of faith. At one time.
The Buddha is the accomplishment of the person (*pudgala-siddhi*). Śrāvastī and the Jeta Grove are the accomplishment of the place (*sthāna-siddhi*).

As for the non-enumeration of the accomplishment of the assembly (*parṣad-siddhi*), it is simply because the text is abbreviated; one should know that there must necessarily have been a group of listeners, as inferred from the later passage which states:

"The fourfold assembly of disciples rejoiced and practiced accordingly. Furthermore, "hearing" (*śruta*) is discussed according to four meanings, extending even to the discussion of the four [aspects] regarding the place.
Earth. Furthermore, the contemplation of the mind, the clarity of hearing, and so forth are not set forth in detail here; they may be understood through the power of one's own insight.

△ Second, the Specific Introduction (Pratyutpanna-nidāna), also called the Prologue of Origination. As each sutra has its own distinct introduction, it is termed the "Specific Introduction. For these reasons:
It is called "Initiation" because it inspires the sacred teachings. The text is divided into six sections. First is Maudgalyāyana’s Attainment of the Path:
Mahāmaudgalyāyana has just attained the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
"Venerable One," [the name] "Nyagrodha" is the name of a tree in the Western Regions. His parents prayed to this tree and obtained him as their son; thus, he was named after it.
"Mahā" is the Sanskrit term, which here translates as "great," "much," or "superior. He is called "Great" because he is revered by celestial kings and great beings.
He is called "Much" because he has universally mastered both internal and external scriptures. He is called "Superior" because he transcends the ninety... [nine hundred?].

Because he surpassed the five kinds of non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthika), he is called "Victorious" (Jina). Here, he is briefly referred to as "Great" (Mahā) to encompass his many superior qualities.
Maudgalyāyana is translated as "Bean-Gatherer" (Śaradvatīputra); this is the clan name of the Venerable One. As this clan was noble, many people addressed him by his surname.
Among the ten great disciples, he was foremost in supernormal powers (abhijñā). Regarding the six supernormal powers: first, the divine eye; second, the divine [ear]...
1. The divine eye (divyacakṣus) clearly perceives all forms, both internal and external, without obstruction. 2. The divine ear (divyaśrotra) fully hears the voices of humans and non-humans. 3.

Knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) understands the distinctions among the various mental states of others. 4. Knowledge of past lives (pūrvanivāsānusmṛti) recollects and recognizes events from former kalpas.
5. The power of spiritual transformation (ṛddhividhi) manifests various miraculous transformations. 6. Knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣayajñāna) realizes them as they truly are.

Regarding the suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path: these six are all called "supernormal powers" (*abhijñā*). "Supernormal" (*shen*) refers to the celestial mind; "power" (*tong*) refers to the nature of wisdom.
It is innate wisdom that illuminates all things with unimpeded penetration. As for the phrase "initially attained":

although the nature of the six powers is inherently possessed by all, it does not manifest due to delusion and must be revealed through cultivation. Now, the Venerable One and Śāriputra have heard the cause for the first time.
Due to the profound meaning of the conditions, he suddenly shattered the delusions of view and realized the stage of *srotāpanna*. He immediately came to see the Buddha;
with the words "Welcome," he received the precepts. Then, just as he had previously seen, he observed again and again, whereby he attained untainted liberation from within his tainted mind.
The wisdom of liberation arises; that which was previously unattained is now attained, and is thus called "initially acquired.

This refers to the realization of the three fruits of liberation—accompanied by wisdom and free from doubt—by relying on the power of the three types of fourfold foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna): those based on nature, those shared with others, and those based on objects.
Therefore, the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) surpass all other śrāvakas. Regarding these six supernormal powers...
Regarding the fact that these qualities are all inherently complete: it is like a person of old who was so intently focused on reading that he did not notice the passing of time until dusk.
Even as twilight fell, he continued to recite with clear clarity. Another person entered from outside and said, "The sky has already grown dark;
why are you still reciting in the darkness? Upon hearing these words, a discriminating mind arose within him, and he immediately became dazed and lost.
See! You should know that the nature of the divine eye is inherently possessed by all people; it is only because of deluded thoughts and discrimination that it fails to manifest before them.
It is like a person suffering from hyperacusis who hears ants crawling under their bed and mistakes them for the sound of chariots, horses, and battle.

This is the inherent nature of the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*). To lose this and become confused regarding the nature of wisdom, thereby regarding it as a disease, is like parents who, though their young child cannot yet speak, intuitively understand the child's intent;
this is the inherent nature of the mind of others (*para-citta-jñāna*). That which has passed since yesterday is still remembered today;
by analogy with what is near, one can certainly recall the distant past; this is the inherent nature of recollecting former lives (*pūrva-nivāsānusmṛti*). It is like Li Guang shooting at a stone...

Feathers fell from the sky. A woman of the Ge clan threw herself into the furnace and became gold; she lifted an iron bowl and found it not heavy, yet as soon as she gave rise to a thought, she could no longer bear its weight.
She forgot her incense box within the hall, and only upon returning did she realize the door was firmly locked. Thus, the nature of supernormal powers (ṛddhi-pāda) is inherently complete.
The clear spring of skulls has been vomited up; it cannot be drunk again. Having heard the words of the ghosts demanding their debts, how could one think of one’s children once more?
Although the nature is inherently complete and untainted, it is merely due to accumulated delusions from which one does not return, burying the spiritual essence.

This causes what is seen not to transcend form and what is heard not to go beyond sound. Furthermore, because one fails to realize the inherent virtues of this nature, one takes circuitous paths in practice, thereby causing—
Supernormal powers (abhijñā) manifest in many varieties. The five supernormal powers acquired as a karmic retribution by devas, nāgas, spirits, and ghosts have narrow scope and limited efficacy.

Those acquired through cultivation by ordinary worldlings and non-Buddhists likewise lack superior utility. Since their outflows (āsrava) are not yet exhausted, they lose these powers when they regress from meditative concentration (dhyāna).
The person liberated through wisdom merely exhausts all outflows, yet the five supernormal powers are not manifested. The person liberated both ways possesses all six supernormal powers;

even within the path of skillful means, they still maintain deliberate mental application (*manasikāra*), whereas the transformation of the unconditioned (*avyākṛta-nirmāṇa*) truly belongs to the ultimate cause.
Although the heterodox and the orthodox are thus distinguished, and the Small and the Great are differentiated, they all collectively rely upon the power of the majestic spirit of inherent virtue.
If these were not inherently possessed, how could cultivation ever achieve completion? To cultivate while being ignorant of one's nature leads to the heterodox or the Small;

it is like a blind person who, though unable to see the solar disk, nevertheless benefits from its illumination. To realize that cultivation resides within nature leads to the Orthodox or the Great; it is like a person with eyes.

The sunlight shines brightly, revealing various forms and colors. Now, regarding the six supernormal powers attained by Maudgalyāyana, his traces are similar to those of the provisional and the small vehicles;
yet his fundamental reality is inconceivable. There is a sutra which says:
"Maudgalyāyana enters eight thousand samādhis and can know the affairs within eight thousand worlds, even shaking eight thousand worlds. Śāriputra enters ten thousand..."
As for samādhi, Kāśyapa is able to enter twelve thousand samādhis. With the exception of two individuals, all other great śrāvakas fall short of Maudgalyāyana;
as for bodhisattvas of the ten stages, they are progressively and manifoldly superior, beyond the reach of thought.
There is no virtue that is not inherently endowed; therefore, one cultivates in accordance with this nature, and thus its wondrous function becomes great.
△ Second, knowing the debt of gratitude and wishing to repay it: desiring to deliver one's parents and repay the kindness of their nursing.

The father gives birth and the mother nurtures; their kindness is immeasurable. To speak of its essentials, it is enough to say that for the mere act of suckling, if one does not contemplate repaying this debt of gratitude, one is no different from a non-human being.
Not to bring them across to liberation is not true repayment of gratitude. Thus, although at first one was mindful of gratitude in every thought-moment, one lacked the power to repay it;
now that one has attained the Way, one must necessarily deliver one's parents first. △ Third, Longing and Yearning.
He searched everywhere.
Then, with his eye of the Path, he surveyed the world.

As soon as the fruit of sainthood was first realized, he immediately observed the place where his parents were born, and in order to fulfill his original vow, he attended to this most urgent priority.
Furthermore, the heavenly eye is obtained through the realization of the Path; therefore, it is called the "Path-eye" (*mārga-cakṣus*).

As for the "worldly," the three realms constitute the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*), while the six destinies and four modes of birth constitute the sentient-being world (*sattva-loka*). △ Fourth, seeing their locations.
He saw his deceased mother reborn among the hungry ghosts (*preta*), unable to find food or drink, her skin and bones standing together in emaciation.
As she gazed upon the world, she was not merely searching for her mother; rather, her father had already attained happiness, so there was no need to mention him.

Her mother, born as a hungry ghost, suffered intensely, hanging upside down. It was from this that he conceived the intention to initiate the excellent method for providing relief. These hungry ghosts are the result of karmic maturation (*vipāka*).

The fruit that compensates for the projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*) is the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*). Not seeing food, drink, and so forth, is the fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*), which compensates for the completing karma (*paripūraka-karman*).
Although the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta-gati*) is the same, there are differences in the experience of retribution: some have no wealth, some have little wealth, and some have wealth.

These three types each have three sub-varieties, forming nine kinds in total. Now, Maudgalyāyana’s mother accumulated the heavy karma of stinginess and greed, thereby inviting the state of having no wealth.
This is the severe retribution. With skin and bone barely joined, one brings calamity upon oneself. A filial son or a compassionate parent—how could they possibly take one’s place?
The evidence of karmic retribution is like a shadow following a form or an echo responding to a sound. It is created solely by the mind; matters do not arise from another.
△ Fifth, lamenting and seeking to rescue the deceased.
Maudgalyāyana was filled with sorrow; he immediately took his alms bowl, filled it with rice, and went to provide food for his mother.
His "sorrow" refers to a grief so profound it penetrates to the very marrow of his bones, a wailing that shook heaven and earth.
Since his mother could not see any food or drink, he first went with the rice in his bowl to rescue her from the extreme suffering of hunger and thirst.
The six evil habits are difficult to transform.

When the mother obtained a bowl of rice, she shielded the bowl with her left hand and tried to grasp the food with her right hand; before the food had even entered her mouth, it transformed into glowing embers, so that she was ultimately unable to eat.

Originally, due to stinginess and greed, I fell into this intense suffering. My habitual nature is difficult to reform, and I ultimately do not turn my heart away from it. Fearing that other ghosts might snatch it away, I guard my bowl;
calculating my food, I seek only the satiation of my own body. Who would have known that the myriad dharmas are but the mind?
The power of karma is exceedingly great; exquisite food suddenly turns into glowing coals.

Had he, at that moment, been able to give rise to a heart of compassion and equanimity, mindful of the suffering shared by his fellow beings and unable to bear consuming it alone, nectar would surely have overflowed, and both himself and others would have been liberated from the wheel of suffering.
Alas, because he did not eliminate the evil causes, the retribution for evil is now so severe. Even with great supernatural powers and profound filial piety, [he cannot escape].
"There is nothing that can be done. [End of section. Part Two:
The Main Body of the Teaching, in three sections. First: Maudgalyāyana weeps in grief and presents his plea. Second: The Tathāgata extensively reveals the essential points of the Dharma.
Third: The disciple attains benefit and is liberated from suffering. Now, the first section.
Maudgalyāyana cried out loudly; wailing with grief and shedding tears, he hurried back to inform the Buddha, recounting everything as it had occurred.
Maudgalyāyana was renowned as the foremost in supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*);

he could transform weapons into celestial flowers, overturn the great earth to take its essence, shake the world-system, and turn back the sun and moon—all of which were not difficult for him. Now, having exhausted all his [powers]...
Despite his supernatural powers and filial devotion, he was ultimately unable to save his mother from her peril; thus, he cried out in profound grief and hurried to inform the Buddha.
Since this account contains no rebukes or disparagements, it serves as an introductory lead-in. Therefore, one should know that this is a gateway of the Mahāyāna teachings. Part Two:

The Tathāgata’s Extensive Demonstration of the Essential Dharma (divided into two sections): First, the Preliminary Demonstration; Second, the Main Demonstration. Regarding the first, the Preliminary Demonstration, there are five further points.
First, the mother’s transgression was revealed as profound.
The Buddha said, "Your mother’s transgressions are deeply rooted and firmly bound.

That which is produced by body and speech is called 'transgression' (*āpatti*); that which is the basis for the karma created in the mental ground is called the 'root' (*mūla*). This has accumulated over a long period."
The accumulation [of afflictions] is called "depth. When their habitual nature becomes firm and solid, making them difficult to reform, they are called "fetters" (*saṃyojana*).
This is evidenced by the analogy of using the left hand to shield a bowl while the right hand gathers food. △ Second, explaining that the power of the child is weak.
"It is not that you alone are powerless.
Śrāvakas have attained mastery over the mind, but have not yet attained mastery over the Dharma;
therefore, their supernatural power cannot alter the fixed karma of their mother. This passage subtly conveys a sense of censure. △ Third, the refutation of heterodoxy.
"Even though your filial piety moves heaven and earth, neither the celestial deities and terrestrial spirits, nor the demons, heterodox practitioners, Daoist masters,
or the gods of the Four Heavenly Kings can do anything about it."
Those who have not yet entered the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) are collectively termed "erroneous.
Although one might combine all the powers of supernatural penetration (*abhijñā*) within the three realms, they would still not equal the power of a single Maudgalyāyana.

Now, by first singling out Maudgalyāyana and subsequently singling out the heavenly deities and others, this is a provisional comparison based on relative magnitude; its true intent is to manifest the greatness of the power of the Saṃgha. △
Fourth, to manifest the power of the correct Dharma:
one must rely on the majestic spiritual power of the Sangha of the ten directions to attain liberation.
"The ten directions" implies that it is not like Maudgalyāyana, who was but a single person; "the Sangha" implies that it is not like the celestial deities and others.
They are not the companions of the sages. Therefore, their majestic spiritual power is inconceivable; it can cause even deeply rooted karmic offenses to be liberated from this point onward.
"Seng" (Saṃgha) is a Sanskrit term; in its full form, it is *saṃgha*. This translates here as "the harmonious assembly."

There are two meanings of "harmony" (saṃgha): first, harmony in principle, which refers to the collective realization of the unconditioned state of cessation through discernment (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha);

second, harmony in practice, which refers to the harmony of precepts in joint cultivation, harmony of views in shared understanding, harmony of benefits in equal distribution, harmony of body in dwelling together, harmony of speech in the absence of contention, and harmony of mind in mutual joy.
Whether consisting of four persons or even an infinite number, such a group is called the Saṃgha. Now, it is said...
"Saṃgha" is a compound term combining the Chinese and Sanskrit. It uses "zhòng" (multitude) to represent number and "sēng" (assembly) to represent virtue.
That which possesses both the harmony of principle and phenomena is called the "true Saṃgha. That which possesses only the harmony of phenomena is called the "pure Saṃgha.
The true Jewel of the Saṃgha can cause the ultimate True Dharma to abide long and not perish; the pure Jewel of the Saṃgha can cause the worldly...
The worldly Dharma remains for a long time without perishing. Therefore, the Vinaya-piṭaka states:

"As long as there are at least five persons who uphold the Vinaya and dwell together in harmony within the world, it is called the non-perishing of the True Dharma. One should know that this refers to the period after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.

The life-vein of the Buddha-Dharma is entirely entrusted to the Sangha; thus, making offerings to the Sangha is equivalent to making universal offerings to the Triple Gem, which is why its majestic power is exceptionally venerable.
Furthermore, for four reasons, the community of monks must necessarily exist: first, because they constitute the noble assembly of the Buddha-Dharma.

First, because the entire world delights in hearing it. Second, by relying on the precepts for cultivation and practice, one becomes a worthy field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), thereby generating goodness in sentient beings.

Third, it correctly rectifies the karma of stinginess among hungry ghosts (*preta*) and universally makes offerings to the ten directions, thereby transforming evil habits. Fourth, the Buddha-dharma is established by means of the Sangha;
thus, this is the most excellent way to manifest the Three Jewels as a single essence. Furthermore, ordinary people gather together from the ten directions...
The holy ones interact and interpenetrate; this is most clearly manifested in the *dharmatā* of the same essence. △ Fifth, the permission to employ salvific methods:
"I shall now expound the methods of salvation, so that all who face difficulties may be freed from sorrow and suffering."

I already know that the Sangha possesses majestic spiritual power; however, I do not yet understand how such resonance is achieved. Therefore, it is necessary to explain the method of "harmonizing with what is above" to fulfill this aspiration of compassion.
Only when the path of response and invocation intersect will one finally attain deliverance. As for the term "all":

in terms of persons, it means benefiting beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, not merely the mother of Maudgalyāyana; in terms of the Dharma, it means eternally uprooting the two types of death, not merely [the suffering of the three evil realms].
Regarding the calamities of hungry ghosts: "sorrow" (*yō*) refers to what is experienced by the mind, while "suffering" (*ku*) refers to what is experienced by the body.

To fear future retribution is called sorrow; to be afflicted by present conditions is called suffering. To lack the means for deliverance is called sorrow; to feel pain as if it were cutting the skin is called suffering.
Upon the single proclamation of this Dharma gate, all shall be enabled to distance themselves from these states. Part Two: The Correct Instruction, in two sections. First, teaching filial piety.
The method for a filial son to present offerings; second, the ritual for the monastic community to receive offerings.
First, regarding the method for a filial son to present offerings, there are five parts. The first is determining the auspicious time.

The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana: "On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, when the Saṃgha of the ten directions holds its *pravāraṇā*, the fifteenth day of the seventh month marks the completion of the ninety-day period of the three-month summer retreat, which began on the sixteenth day of the fourth month.
As they are about to set out on their travels, the members of the Saṃgha assemble in harmony to collectively receive the *pravāraṇā*. This is called *pravāraṇā*."
The term *pravāraṇā* in Sanskrit is translated as "according to one's wish" (*suīyì*).

This means to follow others among three matters, freely raising [points of concern] in the sense of declaring offenses and removing transgressions. The older translation, "self-indulgence" (*zìzì*), is merely a semantic rendering.
The formula states: "Venerable Sangha, today is the day of *pravāraṇā*. I, the bhikṣu [Name], also [participate in] the *pravāraṇā*."
"Grant me leave. If you see, hear, or suspect any offense, O Virtuous Elders, please speak to me out of compassion. If I see my offense, I shall confess it according to the Dharma.
Each person repeats this three times in succession. Once the *pravāraṇā* has been received, it is said that the business of the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*) is concluded;
from this point on, each may go as they please to the east or west. It is only on this day that the great assembly is in harmony.
Exhort one another to revere and uphold the path of practice; because it is a day for reforming faults and turning toward goodness, it is called a "Victorious Time.
△ Second, generating the superior resolve:
One should act for the sake of the parents of seven lifetimes past, as well as those parents currently undergoing calamities and hardships.
The person for whom this is done does not suffer misfortune and hardship for only a single lifetime; such suffering extends through both life and death.

Because one resolves to provide equal relief to all, it is called "Superior Intention" (*śreyas-citta*). However, the mention of "seven generations" is merely a brief statement made from the perspective of the limited mental capacity of ordinary beings.
If one has deep faith in the field of merit and extensively cultivates superior offerings, a most supreme and exalted resolve will arise.

O Mind, you should know that if, even prior to a *rajas-kalpa* (dust-point eon), one’s biological parents and six kinds of close relatives can all together emerge from the wheel of suffering, only then is it called "all difficulties being overcome" and "all sorrow and suffering being left behind. △ Third, making supreme offerings.
Prepare meals consisting of the hundred flavors and the five fruits; provide water-jars for drawing and pouring, fragrant oil, lamps and candles, couches, mats, and bedding.
Place all the world’s sweet and delicious things within these vessels and offer them to the assembly of virtuous monks of the ten directions.

The two characters "equipped with food" (jùfàn) serve as a general heading for the presentation of offerings. "A hundred flavors" expresses the extreme abundance of those flavors, referring to rice, cakes, parched grain, ghee, curd, clarified butter, and so forth.
"Five fruits" refers to roots, stalks, leaves, flowers, and fruits. "Watering vessels" refers to basins and containers.
This refers to the implements for washing the hands, rinsing the feet, and bathing; all must be pure. Incense may be burned as an offering, and oil may be applied to the feet.
*Ding* (錠) means a lamp; that which has a stand is called a *ding*, while that without a stand is called a *deng* (鐙).

Since *deng* and *deng* (燈) are synonymous, the Buddha Rāśmiprabha is sometimes translated as *Dingguang* (錠光), as their meanings are identical. All the sweet delicacies of the world [should be offered], yet one must not become attached to them.
"Within the basin" reiterates the intent of offering the basin and providing sustenance. "Delicious" refers simply to the hundred flavors and five fruits.
"Exhausting the world" means that if wealthy, one arrays the rare treasures of the entire world; if poor, one exhausts the strength and resources of a single person.
It must be done with sincerity and earnestness, without stinginess or parsimony. "Basin" refers to various kinds of pure bowls prepared according to the Dharma.

Bowl offerings—whether a hundred, a thousand, or even countless in number—are arranged in rows as an act of worship; these are collectively termed *pen*, which refers to what is known as the *Ullambana-pen*.
Among the four types of requisites, medicine is omitted for brevity; among the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), music as well as scattered flowers are omitted for brevity.
According to the *Jiguī zhuan* (Record of Returning Home), these should also be included. Thus, one makes offerings to the ten [directions].

Regarding the "Method for the Great Virtuous Assembly of Monks": this teaches the method of mental visualization (*bhāvanā*). The Dharma-realm is without obstruction; even a single atom is not separated from it.
The assembly of the pure ocean-like multitude gathers here within. The offerings manifested before one pervade all lands as numerous as motes of dust;
their unimpeded adornments are layered and inexhaustible, exactly as described in the verses for the visualization of incense and flowers, which should be understood in detail. △
Fourth, praising the supreme field of merit:
on this day, all the noble assembly—some were in mountain retreats practicing meditative concentration; some had attained the fruits of the four paths;

some were walking in meditation beneath trees; some possessed mastery of the six supernormal powers and were teaching and transforming śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; or [others were] bodhisattvas of the ten stages...
The Great Being, manifesting as a bhikṣu by skillful means, was among the great assembly; all were of one mind, receiving the *pātra-bhara* meal.
Possessing the path of the noble community and pure precepts, his virtue was vast and boundless.
On this day—precisely the fifteenth day of the seventh month—it is the supreme time for the gathering of those of highest virtue.
All the assemblies of sages possess vast and profound roots of merit; prior to this day, they each remain in secluded retreat, and after this day, they travel without fixed destination.
Yet, at this auspicious assembly, as they gather like clouds from the great ocean, it is felt to be even more exceptionally sublime.
In mountain valleys and beneath trees, the basic locations upon which he relied are briefly cited; these are sufficient to manifest the excellence of the dhūta practices.

Regarding meditative concentration and walking meditation, the aspects of his cultivation are briefly clarified; these are sufficient to manifest the supreme merit of his diligence. As for those who have attained the fruits of the four paths:

having severed the afflictions of conceptual discrimination, they realize the stage of *srotāpanna*, which is termed the "Path of Vision" (*darśana-mārga*). Having severed six grades of the innate afflictions of the desire realm, they realize...
The Sakṛdāgāmin further severs the remaining three grades of the lower [defilements] and realizes the state of Anāgāmin; this is called the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Having severed the seventy-two grades of innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) of the Form and Formless Realms until they are exhausted, one realizes the state of Arhat;

this is called the Path of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), wherein self-benefit is perfected. One who possesses mastery over the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and teaches Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas governs [the community].

The Great Assembly instructs its disciples to practice the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, thereby attaining liberation by means of the Śrāvaka Vehicle and the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, and accomplishing the benefit of others. As for the great beings who are Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages:
From the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) up to the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), one partially realizes the *dharmakāya*, destroys ignorance, and attains the Middle Way.
One then responds to the fundamental principle by flowing into the nine realms to extensively deliver sentient beings;

though there are none among the six paths and four modes of birth that are not manifested, the Bhikṣu is especially manifested because he sustains the Sangha Jewel and is intimately connected to the Buddha-dharma, as was the case with Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva.

Śākyamuni, assuming the form of a śrāvaka, entered the great assembly. The World-Honored One extensively praised his meritorious virtues and benefits, stating that they surpassed those of all the great bodhisattvas by an incalculable degree.
Having offered this praise, he preached the *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra* as a final exhortation for the末法 (final dharma) age:
"One must not treat renunciants with contempt, disdain, or insult simply because they have shaved their hair and donned dyed robes."

This is the banner and sign of the noble ones. Even if one has broken the precepts or is without them, and upon casting off the body will certainly fall into hell, such a person remains a field of merit for devas and humans;
how much more so for one who possesses the full precepts, and how much more so for one who has realized the fruits of the path?

Therefore, great beings—the Bodhisattvas—for the sake of protecting the True Dharma, frequently manifest as bhikṣus, mingling among ordinary companions; whether acting in opposition or in accord, they act with total freedom according to the capacities of sentient beings.
I shall employ skillful means to transform them, so that those of overweening pride and the faithless may understand that the distinction between the holy and the mundane is unfathomable;
thus they will not dare to look upon ordained disciples with the contemptuous eyes of cattle or sheep, thereby incurring grave transgressions. Through this expedient, [the goal is achieved].
This ensures that the lineage of the Sangha Jewel remains unbroken, upon which the Buddha-Dharma relies for its long-term preservation.

Those "among the great assembly" refer generally to the virtuous dwelling among mountains or beneath trees, companions in meditative concentration and walking practice, individuals who benefit both themselves and others, and those belonging to either the provisional or the ultimate [teachings];
all are gathered together within the Great Assembly of the Pravāraṇā. They are all alike.

"Single-mindedly" (*ekacitta*) refers to one who receives *pātrabharana* food out of compassion for the donor, remaining free from attachment and greed, and neither increasing nor diminishing their regard for whether the food is fine or coarse;

thus it is called "single-minded. In the Sanskrit language, *pātrabharana* is rendered as *pātrabhalana* in the *Svavowed Sūtra* (*Pratimokṣa-sūtra*), which is merely a variation in the weight of the Sanskrit vowels.
This is translated here as "food at will" (*svacchanda-bhojana*), referring to the fifteenth day of the seventh month.
To provide food as an offering to the Buddha and the Sangha is called *pātra-bhara* (alms-food); this refers to the superior offerings listed in the preceding text.

The phrase "possessing pure precepts, etc. concludes by praising the characteristics of the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). Although the noble assembly is unequal in terms of provisional and ultimate [attainments], [it remains a field of merit].
