In sum, the precepts constitute its very essence. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one takes the precepts as one’s teacher and dwells in reliance upon them.

Through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and walking meditation (*caṅkrama*), the four fruits of arhatship and the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) naturally arise from the precepts giving rise to concentration, and concentration giving rise to wisdom (*prajñā*).

Internally concealing the status of a Bodhisattva while externally manifesting as a Śrāvaka, one must especially maintain the prohibitive precepts and strictly guard one’s dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*). Should the precepts not...

Purity is called "shamelessness" (or, in this context, the absence of moral dread). To receive such superior offerings of faith while lacking this purity is no different from swallowing molten copper or iron balls.
If the root of one's precepts is pure, even if one has not yet realized the fruits of the path, one is still called a member of the Noble Assembly (*āryasaṃgha*).

This is because the pure discipline (*saṃvara*) obtained at the time of ascending the altar is itself the untainted body of precepts (*anāsrava-śīlakāya*); it remains essentially unchanged until the attainment of enlightenment.
Such noble virtue gathers like a vast cloud; who could fathom its limits? △ Fifth, the supreme benefit of protection:
Those who make offerings to such monks who observe the *pravāraṇā* will, in this present life, cause their parents and six types of close relatives to attain liberation.

The sufferings of the three miserable realms shall be liberated at that very moment. Clothing and food will appear spontaneously. If one’s parents are still living, they shall enjoy blessings and happiness for a hundred years.
If one’s ancestors of the seven generations have been reborn in heaven, they shall attain sovereign mastery as transformation-born beings and enter the Flower Radiance Heaven.
"Supreme benefit" refers to the two benefits of extraction and bestowal. To emerge from the three miserable realms and attain liberation is the benefit of extracting suffering.

For clothing and food to appear spontaneously, for one to enjoy blessings and happiness for a hundred years, and to enter the Flower-Radiance Heaven is the benefit of bestowing joy. "The present life" refers to the current birth.
With respect to the seven generations mentioned below, "six relations" refers to father, mother, brothers, and sisters;

furthermore, the six relations on the father's side refer to paternal uncles, cousins, brothers, and sons and grandsons; the six relations on the mother's side refer to paternal aunts, maternal aunts, sisters, and daughters and granddaughters.
"Relatives" refers to spouses, male and female servants, concubines, as well as all other distal and proximate affines. Regarding food, clothing, and self—
However, this has merely been a brief enumeration of the joyful matters of humans and devas.

If one were to fully realize their ultimate extent, there would be the garments of shame and modesty, the robes of the Tathāgata, the food of dhyāna-joy and the joy of the Dharma, and the food of the primary truth—all of which are spontaneously present.

As for those who are born through transformation by their own mastery, the various devas do not arise from a womb; if one were to fully realize their ultimate extent, there would be the three kinds of mind-made bodies, all of which are spontaneously...
Regarding "entering the Radiance of Heavenly Flowers": the radiance of exquisite flowers refers to the signs of the bliss of the various devas.

If one fulfills this principle to its ultimate extent, then the myriad practices constitute the flowers, Prajñā constitutes the radiance, the Ultimate Truth constitutes the heavens, and the secret treasury of the three virtues is realized.

It is considered their secure dwelling; this is called "Entering the Radiance of Celestial Flowers. According to this single passage, it is not only that one’s parents are delivered, but also one's six types of relatives and kinsmen;
it is not only that hungry ghosts are rescued, but all are caused to forever leave the three miserable realms.
Not only does it recommend the salvation of the deceased, but it can also benefit those currently living. Its merit is vast and profound, inconceivable.
Therefore it is said: "It causes all who encounter difficulties to be free from sorrow and suffering. △ Second, the ritual for instructing the assembly of monks in receiving offerings.

At that time, the Buddha commanded the Sangha of the ten directions: "First, perform a blessing for the sake of the donor's family, wishing that their parents of seven generations may practice the mind of meditative concentration;
only then should you receive food. When first receiving the food, one should first place it before the Buddha.
Within the monastery, after the Sangha has finished the blessing before the Buddha, one may then personally receive the food.

When a donor provides an offering, it is originally for the sake of one's parents; therefore, before receiving the food, one must first perform a prayer of aspiration (*pariṇāmanā*) and practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
As for the prayer of aspiration, it is the wish that one’s parents may be free from suffering and attain happiness; the text here is abbreviated.

The purpose of practicing meditative concentration is to gather the mind in visualization, fixing the attention and clarifying the spirit so that the prayer of aspiration may be fulfilled. "Before the Buddha" means:
Whichever Buddha image it may be—whether the image before the Buddha in a stupa or monastery, or an image within a pagoda or hall—one should first make offerings to the Buddha and then to the Sangha.
Furthermore, by adding incantations, vows, and meditative concentration, the Three Jewels are fully realized, causing the merit of the offering to be perfected.
△ Third, the recipient attains benefit and liberation from suffering, which has two parts. First, the filial son attains the Dharma.
They were gladdened and benefited, and were liberated from sorrow, grief, and suffering.
At that time, the bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana and the assembly of great bodhisattvas were all filled with great joy; yet Maudgalyāyana wept with a sound of lamentation.
His mind was set at ease and his afflictions were extinguished.
The benefit of the joy of the Dharma was shared by the entire assembly, for each harbored a heart of gratitude.
Maudgalyāyana’s suffering of grief was suddenly relieved, for he knew that his compassionate mother would surely be able to attain liberation. II. The Compassionate Mother Attains Salvation.
[This] brings about deliverance and benefit. One is liberated from the suffering of karmic retribution.
On that very day, Maudgalyāyana’s mother was delivered from the suffering of a hungry ghost for one kalpa.

Her accumulated sins and heavy calamities were such that her lifespan was as long as the creation [of the world]; yet, as soon as the sound of the Dharma was proclaimed, her retribution was extinguished. It was just like the case of Wei... [text ends].
Tí heard the Dharma-door of the Sixteen Contemplations for the first time and suddenly attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Since his compassionate mother had already been liberated from the wheel of suffering, it was fitting that the filial son continued to perform superior offerings. To increase her supreme happiness—what principle could hinder this?

An old tradition states that one must wait until the fifteenth day of the seventh month to offer to the monks at the end of the retreat (*pravāraṇā*) before the mother can be freed from suffering; I fear this is a failure to understand the text, as we rely solely on the present passage.
This further clarifies the excellence of the Dharma-gate.
III. The Section on Circulation has three parts: first, the request; second, the praise and response; third, the practice and dedication. Now, the first:
Maudgalyāyana again addressed the Buddha, saying: "My mother, who gave birth to me, has been able to receive the power of the merit of the Triple Gem. The assembly...

"By the power of the Sangha's spiritual majesty, all disciples of the Buddha in future ages should likewise offer the *bōron* (alms bowl) to rescue and deliver their present parents, as well as their parents up to the seventh generation. Would this not be appropriate?"
The gentleman loves his own parents and extends that love to the parents of others; how much more so, then, for the supreme filial piety that transcends the world?

Previously, when my mother was afflicted by grave suffering, its pain pierced my very vitals, and I hastened to inform the Tathāgata, seeking His compassionate rescue. Now that my mother has attained liberation, I inquire again on behalf of the assembly.
It is said that she was able to receive this through the power of the Triple Gem, and it is further said through the majestic spiritual authority of the Sangha.

As for the power [of the Sangha]: although the Sangha is already included within the enumeration of the Triple Gem, it is separately specified here to manifest the existence of the Sangha-gem as the locus upon which the Buddha and Dharma rely.
△ Second, the response by way of praise, which has two parts: first, the praise and consent; second, the actual response.
First: The Buddha said, "Excellent, most excellent is your question. It was precisely what I intended to speak, yet you have asked it now.

It is called "excellent" because it accords with the capacities of all beings below; it is called "most excellent" because it accords with the enlightened mind above. It was precisely what he intended to speak, and yet—
Question: This is truly what is called an excellent question. Part Two: The Direct Answer, which is further divided into four sections. First, the teaching on initiating practice:

"Good son, if there are bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs, kings, crown princes, ministers, grandees, the three dukes and hundred officials, or the myriad commoners, who practice compassion and filial piety, they should all first, for the sake of their present living parents, [perform offerings] beyond..."
On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, the Buddha’s Day of Joy and the Sangha’s day of *pravāraṇā*,

one should place food of a hundred flavors within an *urunda-bhājana* (alms bowl) for the sake of deceased parents up to the seventh generation and offer it to the self-restrained monks of the ten directions.
Whether one is a monastic or a layperson, whether rich or poor, noble or humble, each has a profound debt of gratitude toward their biological parents.

How could one fail to cultivate the practice of filial piety and compassion? If one does not cultivate filial piety and compassion, they are not only not a disciple of the Buddha, but are no longer even a human being.
These practices should all be undertaken first; it is not necessary to wait until one's parents have passed away before doing so. Thus spoke the Buddha.
As for the "Day of the Buddha’s Joy": when the Tathāgata appeared in the world, his primary purpose was to deliver sentient beings.
On this day of *pravāraṇā*, the community of monks instructs and admonishes one another according to the Dharma, mutually supporting each other so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time.

Furthermore, donors are able to cultivate offerings and create merit through this, extensively practicing filial piety and compassion, thereby fulfilling the Buddha’s original intention. For these reasons, it is called the "Day of the Buddha’s Joy."
Furthermore: △ Second, the instruction to make vows:
"I vow that my present parents shall live for a hundred years free from illness and without the afflictions of any suffering or distress;
even down to their ancestors of seven generations, may they leave behind the sufferings of the hungry ghosts and be reborn among humans and devas, where their merit and joy shall be boundless."
May all practices serve as the vanguard. Having cultivated supreme offerings, one must sustain them with supreme vows;
thus, both the living and the deceased will equally benefit, extending through seven generations and even across kalpas as numerous as motes of dust.
This is for the practitioner of vows to expand their own mental capacity. △ Third, teaching constant practice.
These disciples of the Buddha who cultivate filial piety and obedience should, in every moment of thought, constantly remember their parents,

even extending to their parents for seven generations. On the fifteenth day of the seventh month each year, they should always, with filiality and compassion, call to mind the parents who gave them birth,
and prepare the *urabon* (alms-bowl) offering to present to the Buddhas and the Sangha, thereby repaying the profound kindness of the parents' compassionate love and nurturing.

To constantly remember one’s parents and others in every thought-moment is precisely the teaching for cultivating filial piety and compassion. The Way of filial piety and compassion is precisely the contemplation of the mind (*citta*).

If one does not take the contemplation of the mind as the Dharma-offering, it is merely to harbor empty thoughts; even if one were to wail in grief day and night, what ultimate benefit would there be?
If one is indifferent and forgets this mindfulness, then one is not a disciple of the Buddha, and is a rebellious and unfilial person.

Filial piety. In advancing or retreating, one must necessarily examine the mind; this is how the meaning of this passage is explained. The meaning of examining the mind is fully detailed in the original text.
Regarding the fifteenth day of the seventh month each year and so forth, the teachings prescribe the practice of ritual offerings.

One must not cling to the principle and thereby neglect the ritual, nor should one, after performing the offerings for a single year, claim that one's parents have already attained liberation and thus cease the practice.

Furthermore, one should continue to practice. One must know that the kindness of one's parents is infinitely heavy. It is necessary to contemplate this principle in every thought-moment and to bring these matters to mind every year.
For those who have not yet attained liberation, one should cause them to attain liberation; for those who have already attained liberation, one should cause their supreme bliss to increase.
Only then is one called a filial son, and only then does one begin to repay their kindness. △ Fourth, exhortation to receive and uphold [the teaching].
If all disciples of the Buddha should uphold this Dharma:

"receiving with faith" is called "veneration," and "exclusive mindfulness" is called "upholding. This constitutes a dual exhortation to cultivate the two kinds of offerings—those of both phenomena and principle.

"Should" (*yīngdāng*) is a term of admonition. If one does not uphold [the precepts], one is not a disciple of the Buddha. By using "should," its opposite—what "should not" be done—is implicitly revealed.
What "should not" be done constitutes an offense according to the Vinaya; it is what was traditionally called a "prohibition that must be observed.
To fail to observe it is to violate the prohibition, which may also be categorized as belonging to the Vinaya-piṭaka. Thus, the Sūtra is itself the Vinaya, further clarifying this point.
This is for the sake of the Mahāyāna. △ Third, the practice and observance:
At that time, the bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana and the disciples of the fourfold assembly rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The "fourfold assembly" refers to the four groups: first, the initiating assembly; second, the assembly of those who are the primary audience; third, the assembly of those who act as echoes and shadows; and fourth, the concluding assembly.
Regarding the "assembly": there are three reasons for their joy. First, the purity of the speaker; second, the purity of the Dharma taught;
and third, the purity of the benefit obtained. Although the present text does not explicitly clarify the realization of the fruit [of this benefit], it is nonetheless pure.

Yet, when the perfect voice utters a single chant, its secret benefit is inexhaustible. It was as when, at the very beginning, for the sake of Ajñāta-kauṇḍinya, the Three Refuges and Five Precepts were taught;
immediately, immeasurable devas gave rise to the mind of the Great Way, and immeasurable devas attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
How much more so now, with this most excellent Dharma-gate, which even rebukes the holy fruits of the six supernormal powers—how could it be intended merely for humans and devas?
Shenjin: The scriptural text itself is brief, yet its meaning must necessarily contain two kinds of profound benefit—the secret and the indeterminate.
